name: Sweden
traditionNote: A Nordic civil-law system with a distinctive method: statutes are drafted terse and read against their förarbeten — the committee report, the referral to the Council on Legislation and the government bill — which carry a weight in Swedish interpretation that preparatory works have almost nowhere else.
summary: Statutes (lag) are enacted by the single-chamber Riksdag; ordinances (förordning) are issued by the Government under the Instrument of Government or a delegation in a statute; and a great deal of detailed law is made by agencies as föreskrifter under a delegation from an ordinance. All three are published in Svensk författningssamling, which since 1 April 2018 has been published on svenskforfattningssamling.se by the Government Offices — and the electronic version there is the official and authentic one, the printed series having stopped. Agency regulations are published not in SFS but in that agency's own författningssamling, of which there are dozens. Sweden has no constitutional court: courts and public authorities apply the constitutional review rule in Chapter 11 of the Instrument of Government and simply decline to apply a provision that conflicts with a superior norm, while the Lagrådet reviews important bills for constitutionality before they are passed. Precedent works the same way — the rulings of the Högsta domstolen and the Högsta förvaltningsdomstolen are called vägledande, guiding, and are followed without formally binding.
hierarchy: The four fundamental laws — Regeringsformen, Successionsordningen, Tryckfrihetsförordningen and Yttrandefrihetsgrundlagen — amended only by two identical Riksdag decisions with an election in between
Riksdagsordningen, the Riksdag Act, standing between the fundamental laws and ordinary statutes
EU law, applied with primacy since accession in 1995
Myndighetsföreskrifter — binding agency regulations made under delegation, published in each agency's own författningssamling
Kommunala föreskrifter — municipal and regional rules under the Local Government Act, published by the municipality itself

gazette.name: Svensk forfattningssamling
gazette.coverage: The official electronic series from 1 April 2018 onward; statutes issued before that date are in the earlier printed series, digitised elsewhere
gazette.desc: The publication in which a Swedish statute or ordinance is promulgated. The site says what it is in one line: the official and authentic version of statutes, ordinances and certain agency regulations. Everything is cited by SFS number — year and running number, as in 1974:152 for the Instrument of Government — and that number never changes even as the text is amended.
gazette.howto: Search by SFS number, or pick a year and read down the list of SFS-nummer, Rubrik and Publicerad. An amending act appears as its own SFS item titled 'Lag om ändring i …', which is what you want when you need the amendment itself rather than its effect. 'Andra författningssamlingar' leads to the agency collections.
gazette.note: This site holds only what was issued from 1 April 2018 onward. For an older statute, the SFS number still works, but the text has to be found through the Riksdag's collection or the printed series. It answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

constitution.name: Regeringsformen
constitution.authority: Riksdagen; published in Svensk författningssamling as SFS 1974:152
constitution.coverage: In force since 1 January 1975 and substantially reformed in 2011; the consolidated text on the Riksdag site shows the current wording
constitution.desc: The principal of Sweden's four fundamental laws. The other three are the Act of Succession, the Freedom of the Press Act of 1766 — the oldest such law in the world — and the Fundamental Law on Freedom of Expression, and all four together are the constitution. Chapter 11 gives every court and public authority the power to set aside a provision that conflicts with a fundamental law, which is why Sweden needs no constitutional court.
constitution.howto: Read the consolidated text on the Riksdag's document collection, which shows amendments in place; the other three fundamental laws are separate SFS numbers in the same collection. The Riksdag publishes English versions of all four in 'The Constitution of Sweden'.
constitution.note: A fundamental law is amended by two identical decisions of the Riksdag with a general election between them, and a referendum may be demanded on the proposal in between.

sources.name: Dokument och lagar (Riksdagen)
sources.coverage: Statutes and ordinances in consolidated form, government bills, committee reports, written questions, minutes and votes, with the older parliamentary print reachable separately
sources.desc: The database Swedish lawyers actually use for the text of a statute: the SFS text with amendments incorporated, alongside the whole legislative history in one collection. Because Swedish method leans so heavily on preparatory works, having the bill and the committee report beside the statute is not a convenience but the method itself.
sources.howto: Search by SFS number, title or keyword and filter by document type — svensk författningssamling for the statutes, proposition for government bills, betänkande for committee reports. Each statute page shows the amendments made to it; the open data service exposes the same corpus for bulk work.
sources.note: The consolidated texts here are the Riksdag's editorial versions of the SFS. Where wording is critical, the SFS item as promulgated is the authentic text.

sources.name: Lagrummet
sources.en: Portal to Swedish public legal information
sources.coverage: Links to the collections of statutes, agency regulations, guiding court decisions, preparatory works and EU law
sources.desc: The state's own index of where Swedish legal information lives. It exists because the material is scattered by design — statutes with the Government Offices, consolidated texts with the Riksdag, agency rules with each agency, case law with the courts — and this is the map of that scattering.
sources.howto: Use 'Rättskällorna' to browse by category, or the search to find which collection holds a given kind of material; the glossary explains the Swedish terms of art that the categories use.
sources.note: A directory rather than a database: nothing is searched across collections from here.

sources.name: Sok rattspraxis (Sveriges Domstolar)
sources.coverage: Guiding decisions of the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court, the courts of appeal, the administrative courts of appeal and the specialist courts; Supreme Court summaries from 1981 onward and its decisions from 2023 onward
sources.desc: The courts' own service for vägledande avgöranden — the decisions meant to guide. Sweden publishes what is precedential rather than everything, so this is a curated collection by design, not an incomplete one.
sources.howto: Filter by court with the domstolskod parameter or the court picker, then search full text or by case number — Swedish case numbers carry a letter for the type of case, T for civil, B for criminal, Ö for other. The Supreme Court's own pages list the latest decisions and offer an RSS feed.
sources.note: First-instance judgments are generally not published anywhere; they are public documents and are obtained by asking the court's registry for them.

sources.name: Hogsta domstolen
sources.coverage: The Court's own decisions, its grants of leave to appeal, pending references to the Court of Justice of the EU, and explanations of how it publishes
sources.desc: The final instance in civil and criminal matters. Its published decisions are called prejudikat and are cited as NJA year and page for the older reported series, or by case number for the recent ones; alongside it and independent of it sits the Högsta förvaltningsdomstolen for administrative and tax matters.
sources.howto: 'Avgöranden' lists the most recent decisions and links into the Sök rättspraxis service; the Court's page on publication explains which decisions are reported and how they are named. The administrative supreme court has an equivalent section on the same domstol.se site.
sources.note: Leave to appeal is required and rarely given, so most Swedish law is settled in the courts of appeal, whose decisions are published far more selectively.

sources.name: Rattsliga dokument (Regeringen)
sources.coverage: Government bills (propositioner), official inquiry reports (SOU), departmental series (Ds), committee terms of reference (kommittédirektiv) and referrals to the Council on Legislation (lagrådsremisser)
sources.desc: The preparatory works, which in Sweden are not background but part of the argument. A Swedish provision is habitually read together with what the bill said it was for, and the SOU that preceded the bill is often the fullest analysis of the problem the law addresses.
sources.howto: Filter by document type and year, or search by subject; a bill states the SFS numbers it will produce, which is the link between the preparatory work and the statute. The same documents are searchable in the Riksdag's collection, which is often the easier route for older material.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: Andra forfattningssamlingar
sources.authority: Each central agency publishes its own collection; the index is kept by the Government Offices
sources.coverage: Dozens of agency series — among them the tax agency's, the transport agency's, the financial supervisory authority's and the work environment authority's
sources.desc: The layer where most operative Swedish regulation actually lives. An ordinance delegates to an agency, and the agency issues föreskrifter in its own författningssamling, which is binding, is not in SFS, and is often the only place the detailed rule exists.
sources.howto: Find the agency responsible for the field, then its collection from this index, and search there; the agency's abbreviation prefixes the citation, as in SKVFS or TSFS, followed by year and number.
sources.note: Coverage, formats and consolidation vary by agency: some publish consolidated texts, others only the amending regulations. Like the rest of the SFS site, the index answers automated requests with 403.

sources.name: Riksdagens oppna data
sources.coverage: The document corpus — statutes, bills, reports, minutes, votes and members — as downloadable datasets and through a query interface
sources.desc: Sweden publishes its parliamentary and legislative corpus as open data, which makes it one of the easier European legal systems to work with in bulk.
sources.howto: Read the documentation, then build queries against the document endpoints or download the packaged datasets; the document types match the filters used on the public site.

sources.name: The Constitution of Sweden (English)
sources.coverage: The four fundamental laws and the Riksdag Act in English translation
sources.desc: The Riksdag's own English edition of the constitutional texts, published as a volume and kept broadly current — the main piece of Swedish law available in English from the state.
sources.howto: Follow the constitution pages in the English section of the Riksdag site for the texts and the explanatory material; ordinary statutes are generally not translated, and where a ministry has produced a translation it sits on that ministry's own pages.
sources.note: Translations have no legal force. Swedish is the only language in which Swedish law is enacted.

sources.name: EUR-Lex (pa svenska)
sources.authority: Europeiska unionens publikationsbyrå (Publications Office of the European Union)
sources.coverage: EU treaties, legislation, consolidated texts, case law and national implementing measures, in Swedish among the official languages
sources.desc: SFS carries no EU law, and since accession in 1995 a large part of what applies in Sweden is an EU regulation that needed no Swedish statute. Lagrummet lists EU law as one of the Swedish sources of law for exactly this reason.
sources.howto: Search by CELEX number or subject with the interface set to Swedish; the national implementing measures tab on a directive lists the Swedish statutes and ordinances notified for it.
sources.note: The Swedish language version of an EU act is authentic alongside the others; the Official Journal edition is the binding one.

sources.name: lagen.nu
sources.authority: An independent project by a private individual, built on the public sources
sources.coverage: Consolidated statutes with commentary and links to the case law and preparatory works that concern each provision
sources.desc: A free, unofficial reworking of the same public material into something more navigable — each section of a statute shown with the guiding decisions and the passages of the bill that discuss it. Widely used by students and by anyone without a subscription.
sources.howto: Go to the statute by SFS number or name and read section by section; the references beneath each section link to the decisions and preparatory works. Confirm any wording against the Riksdag's text or the SFS item.
sources.note: Unofficial and maintained privately, so it can lag the current wording. It is a finding aid, not a source.

sources.name: JUNO
sources.coverage: Legislation with commentary, the Karnov and Zeteo annotations, case law, journals and practice literature
sources.desc: The subscription service most Swedish firms and courts work in, formed from the merger of the two older commercial products. What it adds to the free sources is the annotation — the lagkommentar tradition that explains a provision section by section.
sources.howto: Access requires a subscription or an institutional login; the free sources above cover the statutes, the preparatory works and the guiding case law.
sources.note: Private and commercial. Nothing here is an official text.

sources.name: Sveriges internationella overenskommelser
sources.coverage: The SÖ series of treaties and agreements Sweden has concluded, with their texts and entry-into-force particulars
sources.desc: Sweden is dualist: a treaty binds the state internationally when ratified, but it applies internally only through a statute that incorporates or transforms it. The SÖ series is the treaty text; the statute that gives it domestic effect is a separate SFS item.
sources.howto: Browse or search the SÖ series by year and number; then look for the incorporating statute in SFS — the European Convention on Human Rights, for example, applies in Sweden through SFS 1994:1219 as well as through the Instrument of Government.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: Justitieombudsmannen
sources.authority: Riksdagens ombudsmän (JO), elected by and reporting to the Riksdag
sources.coverage: Decisions on complaints against public authorities and their staff, published individually and in the annual report (JO:s ämbetsberättelse), going back decades
sources.desc: The oldest ombudsman institution in the world, created in 1809, and in practice the main published commentary on Swedish administrative law: how long an authority may take, what it must disclose, when it may refuse. Its decisions are cited in argument even though they bind nobody.
sources.howto: Search the decisions by subject or authority, or read the annual report for the year; a decision states the authority, the provisions at issue and the criticism made. The Chancellor of Justice (Justitiekanslern) supervises in parallel and publishes separately.
sources.note: JO decisions are criticism, not orders. They cannot change a decision, award compensation or bind a court.

sources.name: Rattslig vagledning (Skatteverket)
sources.coverage: The agency's consolidated guidance on tax law, with its position statements (ställningstaganden), legal comments and the annual guide, updated continuously
sources.desc: Shown here as the pattern for Swedish administrative practice: the substantive rules of a field are set out by the agency that administers it, in guidance that is not binding on courts but decides almost every case that never reaches one. Most Swedish agencies publish an equivalent.
sources.howto: Browse by subject area for the current edition, and look separately at the ställningstaganden, which are the agency's published positions on contested questions and carry the date from which the agency applies them.
sources.note: Guidance, not law. A court is free to disagree with it, and where it conflicts with a statute the statute governs.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of a statute
findLaw.steps: Search the Riksdag's document collection by SFS number or title and open the statute, which is shown with its amendments incorporated and a list of the amending SFS items. Note the SFS number: 1974:152 is the Instrument of Government whatever has been done to it since.

For anything issued from 1 April 2018 onward, search the SFS number on svenskforfattningssamling.se, which serves the official and authentic version. For older statutes, the promulgated text is in the printed series, and the Riksdag's consolidated version with its amendment list is the practical substitute.

findLaw.task: Find out what a provision was meant to do
findLaw.steps: Take the preparatory works: the government bill that produced the provision, and behind it the SOU inquiry report. Both are on the Government Offices' legal documents pages and in the Riksdag's collection. Swedish courts read these as a matter of course, so an argument built without them is incomplete.

Search the courts' Sök rättspraxis service, filtering to the court you need; Supreme Court summaries run from 1981 and its decisions from 2023. Older Supreme Court decisions are cited as NJA with year and page, and the Supreme Administrative Court's as HFD or the older RÅ.

findLaw.task: Find an agency regulation rather than a statute
findLaw.steps: Identify the agency with the delegated power, then open its own författningssamling from the index of other collections. The citation prefixes the agency's abbreviation to a year and number, and the rule will not be in SFS at all.

findLaw.task: Check whether a rule can be set aside as unconstitutional
findLaw.steps: There is no constitutional court and no petition procedure: under Chapter 11 of the Instrument of Government, the court or authority deciding your case may itself refuse to apply a provision that conflicts with a fundamental law. Look for guiding decisions where a court has done so, and for the Council on Legislation's opinion on the bill, which is published with the preparatory works.

findLaw.task: Read Swedish constitutional law in English
findLaw.steps: Use the Riksdag's English edition of the four fundamental laws and the Riksdag Act. For ordinary statutes there is usually no translation at all; where a ministry has commissioned one it sits on that ministry's pages and is unofficial.

subnational: Sweden is a unitary state whose 290 municipalities and 21 regions have taxing power and wide administrative responsibility but no legislative power: what they adopt are föreskrifter, taxor and reglementen under the Local Government Act and under specific statutes — local order rules, waste rules, building charges, school catchments. These are published by the municipality itself, usually in its own author­ity collection on its website, and they are not gathered in any national database, so the municipality's site is the only route to them. Regional and municipal decisions can be challenged by any member of the municipality through laglighetsprövning in the administrative courts, which is where the limits of what a municipality may decide are actually drawn. Sweden's Sámi Parliament is an administrative authority and an elected body, not a legislature; reindeer husbandry law is national law.
caveats: The authentic version of a Swedish statute is the SFS item, and svenskforfattningssamling.se only holds what was issued from 1 April 2018 onward — for anything older, the consolidated text on the Riksdag site is an editorial version of a printed original. Most operative regulation is not in SFS at all but in the agencies' own collections, which vary in whether they consolidate, and municipal rules are published only locally. Case law is published because it is meant to guide: first-instance judgments generally are not online, and their absence tells you nothing. There is no constitutional court, so a provision is not struck down but set aside in a particular case, and it stays on the books afterwards. Preparatory works are central to Swedish interpretation but they are not the law: where the enacted text and the bill diverge, the text governs. English translations exist for the fundamental laws and very little else, and none has legal force.
